description: SQL & Relational Analytics: Window Functions & Retention Cohort Analysis

prompts.statement: Given a table UserLogins with columns (user_id INT, login_date DATE), write a SQL query to find all users who logged in for at least 3 consecutive days. Return the user_id for each qualifying user with duplicates removed, ordered by user_id ascending.
constraints: UserLogins may contain duplicate entries for the same user on the same date
Must run efficiently without Cartesian joins

examples.explanation: User 1 logged in on 3 consecutive days (Sep 1, 2, 3). User 2 skipped Sep 2.

clarificationBranches.question: If a user logs in multiple times on the same day, does that count as multiple consecutive days?
clarificationBranches.answer: No. You must deduplicate (user_id, login_date) pairs before evaluating consecutive date streaks.

followups.question: How would you modify the query to return the length of the longest consecutive login streak for every user?
followups.criterion: Groups by (user_id, streak_group_id), calculates COUNT(*), then takes MAX(streak_length) partitioned by user_id.

privateReference.approach: Use the standard date grouping technique: deduplicate dates with DISTINCT, order dates per user using ROW_NUMBER(), subtract the row number in days from login_date to form a group anchor (login_date - ROW_NUMBER() * INTERVAL '1 day'), then GROUP BY user_id and the anchor with HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3.
checks: Deduplicates multiple logins on the same day
Uses ROW_NUMBER() window function correctly partitioned by user_id
privateReference.expectedComplexity: O(N log N) time for sorting, O(N) memory

packs.title: SQL Practice: Window Functions & Consecutive Streaks
packs.instructions: Write a single performant SQL query. Avoid quadratic self-joins and correctly handle duplicate date records.
